name: IR break beam sensor, 3 mm LEDs
description: Infrared break beam pair: an emitter (IR LED, 2 wires) shines a 10 degree beam across a gap of up to about 25 cm onto a receiver (3 wires) whose open-collector output pulls LOW while the beam is broken and floats (needs a pull-up) while it is intact. Response under 2 ms; runs on 3.3-5.5 V. Sold as: Adafruit IR Break Beam Sensors with Premium Wire Header Ends - 3mm LEDs (product 2167), receiver red/black/white wires plus emitter red/black wires, 230 mm leads with male header ends.
eli5: An invisible light beam across a gap: your board is told the moment something walks through and blocks it.

pins.name: RX_VCC
pins.description: Receiver red wire: supply 3.3-5.5 V. Use the board's 3V3 on an ESP32/Pico, since the signal pull-up goes to this rail.

pins.name: RX_SIG
pins.description: Receiver white (or yellow) wire: open-collector output, LOW = beam broken, HIGH (through the pull-up) = beam intact. Needs a pull-up: 10 kOhm to the red wire, or the GPIO's internal pull-up.

pins.name: EM_VCC
pins.description: Emitter red wire: supply 3.3-5.5 V (about 10 mA at 3.3 V, 20 mA at 5 V; 5 V gives more range)

buildNotes: These are two separate parts on loose 230 mm leads, each ending in a single male header pin: receiver red/black/white and emitter red/black. There are no printed labels; go by wire colour (the signal may be yellow instead of white).
Point the emitter straight at the receiver, at most about 25 cm apart (less at 3.3 V). Their 10 degree beam needs them lined up.
The receiver output is open collector: it needs a pull-up. Fit a 10 kOhm resistor from the white wire to the receiver's red wire, or enable the GPIO's internal pull-up (Pin.PULL_UP).
On an ESP32 or Pico power the receiver (and its pull-up) from 3V3 so the signal never exceeds 3.3 V. The emitter may run from 5 V for longer range.
Signal reads 0 while the beam is broken and 1 while it is intact.
Strong sunlight contains IR and can swamp the receiver outdoors.

driver.code:
# Adafruit IR break beam sensor (3 mm LEDs, product 2167), MicroPython driver.
# The emitter (2 wires: red = power, black = ground) just needs 3.3-5.5 V.
# The receiver (3 wires: red = power, black = ground, white/yellow = signal) has an
# open-collector output: its transistor pulls the signal to ground while the beam is
# broken and lets it float while the beam is intact. A pull-up is therefore required:
# the internal pull-up is enabled here, and a 10 kOhm resistor from the signal wire to the receiver's red wire
# also works (Adafruit guide).
#   signal LOW  (0) -> beam broken (something between emitter and receiver)
#   signal HIGH (1) -> beam intact (receiver sees the emitter)
# Response time < 2 ms.
from machine import Pin


class BreakBeam:
    def __init__(self, pin):
        self.pin = Pin(pin, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP) if isinstance(pin, int) else pin

    def raw(self):
        """Logic level on the signal wire: 0 = broken, 1 = intact."""
        return self.pin.value()

    def broken(self):
        """True while something blocks the beam."""
        return self.pin.value() == 0

    def irq(self, handler, on_break=True):
        """Call handler(pin) when the beam is broken (falling edge) or, with
        on_break=False, when it is restored (rising edge)."""
        trig = Pin.IRQ_FALLING if on_break else Pin.IRQ_RISING
        return self.pin.irq(handler=handler, trigger=trig)

example.code:
from breakbeam import BreakBeam
import time

beam = BreakBeam({RX_SIG})
while True:
    print('Beam: %s' % ('BROKEN' if beam.broken() else 'intact'))
    time.sleep(0.5)

test.title: Reports the beam as broken when something blocks it
